questions.question: What is the definition of the open metric ball $\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)\leq r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \gt r\}$
$\{r\in\mathbb{R}\colon d(r,\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt \boldsymbol{x}\}$

questions.question: In the notation $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$, what does $r$ represent?
options: The centre
The radius
The metric
The whole space

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric, which point belongs to $\boldsymbol{B}(0,1)$?
What is true about open balls?
options: Open balls are always closed and never open.
Open balls are open sets.
Open balls cannot be used to define open sets.
Open balls exist only in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

questions.question: In the discrete metric, what is $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x},0.5)$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\}$
$\varnothing$
The whole space
All points except $\boldsymbol{x}$

questions.question: An open metric ball is $B(x_0,r)=\{x \colon d(x,x_0)<r\}$. Why is the defining inequality $d(x,x_0)<r$ strict rather than $\le$?
options: Because points at distance exactly $r$ are not included.
Because the radius must be negative.
Because the centre point is excluded from every open ball.
Because only boundary points are included.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with usual distance, is $(1,0)$ in $\boldsymbol{B}((0,0),1)$?
options: No, because its distance is exactly $1$, not less than $1$.
Yes, because its distance is equal to the radius.
Yes, because every point on the coordinate axes is included.
No, because the centre must be $(1,0)$.

questions.question: What is $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$ in a metric space?
options: Points with distance from $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ strictly less than $r$.
The set of points with distance exactly $r$.
The set of points with distance greater than $r$.
The set containing only $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: What role do open balls play in metric spaces?
options: Basic building blocks for open sets and continuity.
They replace the metric function entirely.
They are always finite sets.
They contain only boundary points.

questions.question: Which point is not in $B(0,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric?
What union-of-balls characterisation describes open subsets?
options: A subset is open if and only if it contains at least one open ball.
A subset is open if and only if its complement is a union of open balls.
A subset is open if and only if it is a union of closed balls.
A subset is open if and only if it is a union of open balls.

questions.question: If $d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)=r$, is $\boldsymbol{x}$ in $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$?
options: Yes, because equality is allowed in an open ball.
No, because the definition requires $d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt r$.
Yes, because every point at distance $r$ is the centre.
No, because open balls contain no points.
